AI.motivation: Existing quantum divergences rely on classical f-divergences or Renyi-type constructions, which obscure quantum geometric effects and limit understanding of quantum distinguishability.
AI.method: Proposes quantum relative-alpha-entropy that extends Umegaki's relative entropy but falls outside f-divergence class. Uses Nussbaum-Szkola-type distributions to establish exact correspondence with classical relative-alpha-entropy.
AI.result: The divergence exhibits nonlinear convexity, yields generalized convexity for Petz-Renyi divergence for alpha>1, is additive under tensor products, unitary invariant, and depends only on relative geometry of quantum states.
AI.conclusion: Relative-alpha-entropy represents a fundamentally geometric notion of quantum distinguishability not captured by existing divergence frameworks, revealing new quantum geometric effects.

title: Quantum MIMO Channel Modeling in Turbulent Free-Space Optical Links
summary: Free-space optical (FSO) links supporting spatial multiplexing provide a natural physical realization of Quantum MIMO channels. We develop a first-principles model for Quantum MIMO channels derived directly from wave-optical propagation through three-dimensional atmospheric turbulence. The framework explicitly accounts for intermodal crosstalk, finite detection apertures, and the system-bath separation induced by spatial-mode projection. We distinguish between distinguishable and indistinguishable photon regimes, showing that indistinguishability leads to intrinsically many-body interference effects described by matrix permanents. To obtain a completely positive and trace-preserving logical description, we introduce an erasure-extended encoding in which turbulence-induced leakage and photon loss are mapped to flagged erasure states. The resulting Quantum MIMO channel naturally reduces to a correlated n-qubit erasure channel, with correlations arising from the shared turbulent medium. Limiting regimes in which correlated Pauli channels emerge as effective approximations are also identified.

AI.tldr: Quantum MIMO channel model for free-space optical links with spatial multiplexing, derived from wave-optical propagation through atmospheric turbulence, accounting for intermodal crosstalk, finite apertures, and system-bath separation.
AI.motivation: Free-space optical links with spatial multiplexing provide a natural physical realization of Quantum MIMO channels, but existing models lack first-principles derivation from wave-optical propagation through atmospheric turbulence.
AI.method: Developed a first-principles model derived directly from wave-optical propagation through 3D atmospheric turbulence, accounting for intermodal crosstalk, finite detection apertures, and system-bath separation via spatial-mode projection. Introduced erasure-extended encoding to map turbulence-induced leakage and photon loss to flagged erasure states.
AI.result: The model distinguishes between distinguishable and indistinguishable photon regimes, showing indistinguishability leads to many-body interference effects described by matrix permanents. The resulting Quantum MIMO channel reduces to a correlated n-qubit erasure channel with correlations arising from shared turbulent medium. Identified limiting regimes where correlated Pauli channels emerge as effective approximations.
AI.conclusion: The developed framework provides a complete, physically grounded description of Quantum MIMO channels for free-space optical links with spatial multiplexing, enabling analysis of quantum communication performance in realistic atmospheric turbulence conditions.

title: Scalable on-chip integration of diamond color centers for cryogenic quantum photonics
summary: Chip integration of quantum emitters is a crucial milestone for scalable quantum photonic information processing. Among optically active defect centers for quantum photonics, diamond color centers are promising because of their long spin coherence times and high photon emission rates. However, for a coherent-photon emission, they typically require a cryogenic environment to protect optical coherence from thermal phonons, which makes chip integration challenging. In this paper, we develop a chip-integrated diamond photonic crystal cavity embedding an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. We confirm cryogenic operation by observing Purcell enhancement of NV-center emission via an edge-coupled optical fiber. This result demonstrates successful integration of diamond color centers, a photonic crystal cavity, and an optical waveguide-fiber package, representing a key step toward scalable diamond-based quantum communication platforms.

AI.tldr: Chip-integrated diamond photonic crystal cavity with NV centers enables cryogenic operation and Purcell-enhanced emission, advancing scalable diamond quantum photonics.
AI.motivation: Chip integration of quantum emitters is essential for scalable quantum photonic information processing. Diamond color centers (particularly NV centers) are promising due to their long spin coherence times and high photon emission rates, but they typically require cryogenic environments to maintain optical coherence, making chip integration challenging.
AI.method: Developed a chip-integrated diamond photonic crystal cavity embedding an ensemble of nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. Used edge-coupled optical fiber to interface with the system and measure emission properties at cryogenic temperatures.
AI.result: Confirmed cryogenic operation by observing Purcell enhancement of NV-center emission via the edge-coupled optical fiber. Demonstrated successful integration of diamond color centers, photonic crystal cavity, and optical waveguide-fiber package.
AI.conclusion: This represents a key step toward scalable diamond-based quantum communication platforms by successfully integrating the essential components (quantum emitters, cavity, and optical interface) in a chip-compatible format with cryogenic operation.

title: QNAS: A Neural Architecture Search Framework for Accurate and Efficient Quantum Neural Networks
comment: To appear at the IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), Maastricht, The Netherlands, June 2026
summary: Designing quantum neural networks (QNNs) that are both accurate and deployable on NISQ hardware is challenging. Handcrafted ansatze must balance expressivity, trainability, and resource use, while limited qubits often necessitate circuit cutting. Existing quantum architecture search methods primarily optimize accuracy while only heuristically controlling quantum and mostly ignore the exponential overhead of circuit cutting. We introduce QNAS, a neural architecture search framework that unifies hardware aware evaluation, multi objective optimization, and cutting overhead awareness for hybrid quantum classical neural networks (HQNNs). QNAS trains a shared parameter SuperCircuit and uses NSGA-II to optimize three objectives jointly: (i) validation error, (ii) a runtime cost proxy measuring wall clock evaluation time, and (iii) the estimated number of subcircuits under a target qubit budget. QNAS evaluates candidate HQNNs under a few epochs of training and discovers clear Pareto fronts that reveal tradeoffs between accuracy, efficiency, and cutting overhead. Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and Iris benchmarks, we observe that embedding type and CNOT mode selection significantly impact both accuracy and efficiency, with angle-y embedding and sparse entangling patterns outperforming other configurations on image datasets, and amplitude embedding excelling on tabular data (Iris). On MNIST, the best architecture achieves 97.16% test accuracy with a compact 8 qubit, 2 layer circuit; on the more challenging Fashion-MNIST, 87.38% with a 5 qubit, 2 layer circuit; and on Iris, 100% validation accuracy with a 4 qubit, 2 layer circuit. QNAS surfaces these design insights automatically during search, guiding practitioners toward architectures that balance accuracy, resource efficiency, and practical deployability on current hardware.

AI.tldr: QNAS is a neural architecture search framework for hybrid quantum-classical neural networks that jointly optimizes accuracy, runtime efficiency, and circuit cutting overhead under qubit constraints.
AI.motivation: Designing quantum neural networks for NISQ hardware is challenging due to the need to balance expressivity, trainability, and resource constraints, while existing methods primarily optimize accuracy and ignore the exponential overhead of circuit cutting.
AI.method: QNAS trains a shared parameter SuperCircuit and uses NSGA-II multi-objective optimization to jointly optimize validation error, runtime cost proxy, and estimated number of subcircuits under target qubit budget constraints.
AI.result: QNAS discovers clear Pareto fronts revealing tradeoffs between accuracy, efficiency, and cutting overhead. Achieves 97.16% test accuracy on MNIST with 8-qubit 2-layer circuit, 87.38% on Fashion-MNIST with 5-qubit 2-layer circuit, and 100% validation accuracy on Iris with 4-qubit 2-layer circuit.
AI.conclusion: QNAS automatically surfaces design insights about embedding types and entangling patterns, guiding practitioners toward architectures that balance accuracy, resource efficiency, and practical deployability on current NISQ hardware.

title: Complete coherent control of spin qubits in self-assembled InAs quantum dots under oblique magnetic fields
summary: We demonstrate complete coherent control of a single spin qubit confined in a self-assembled InAs negatively charged quantum dot subjected to an Oblique magnetic field, and directly compare this regime with the conventional Voigt geometry. In the Oblique-field configuration, the groundstate spin eigenstates are found to be unequal superpositions of the bare electron spin, with their composition tunable via the orientation of the applied field. This tunable spin mixing provides an additional degree of freedom to engineer the spin basis and associated optical couplings in the charged quantum dot system. Although this geometry has a distinct structure with important implications, it provides a regime in which we can fully and coherently control the tailored spin qubit. We observe Rabi oscillations and Ramsey fringes, and demonstrate arbitrary single-qubit rotations, enabling a direct comparison with the Voigt case. Our results establish that spin-qubit control does not necessarily require a pure Voigt geometry and can instead be achieved under Oblique magnetic fields. This relaxes constraints on device and field alignment and offers a versatile route to design and optimize quantum information processing architectures in semiconductor quantum dots.

AI.tldr: Complete coherent control of a single spin qubit in an InAs quantum dot under oblique magnetic field, demonstrating arbitrary single-qubit rotations and comparing with conventional Voigt geometry.
AI.motivation: To explore spin-qubit control beyond the conventional Voigt geometry, relaxing constraints on device and field alignment while providing additional degrees of freedom for engineering spin basis and optical couplings in quantum dot systems.
AI.method: Used an oblique magnetic field configuration on a self-assembled InAs negatively charged quantum dot, where groundstate spin eigenstates become unequal superpositions of bare electron spin with tunable composition via field orientation. Performed Rabi oscillations, Ramsey fringes, and arbitrary single-qubit rotations.
AI.result: Demonstrated complete coherent control of the tailored spin qubit under oblique magnetic fields, achieving arbitrary single-qubit rotations comparable to Voigt geometry performance. Showed that spin mixing provides additional engineering degrees of freedom for quantum information processing.
AI.conclusion: Spin-qubit control does not require pure Voigt geometry and can be achieved under oblique magnetic fields, relaxing alignment constraints and offering versatile design routes for semiconductor quantum dot quantum information architectures.

title: Postquantum steering in scenarios with multiple characterised parties
comment: Matlab workspaces can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19468921. Comments welcome!
summary:
The study of stronger-than-quantum phenomena (i.e., postquantum) has enabled a deeper understanding of the scope of quantum theory. Much is known about the case of correlations in Bell scenarios, where the device-independent framework allowed us to explore its possibilities independently of the formalism of quantum theory. However, less is known about the phenomenon of Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering. Here, the `characterised parties' are assumed to describe their systems locally through the quantum formalism, which inconveniences a theory-independent description. In addition, a theorem by Gisin and Hughston, Josza and Wootters further hindered the discovery of the phenomenon. The study of postquantum steering, initiated about a decade ago, has been quite fruitful, including: the development of mathematical formalisms that frame the effect, resource theories that quantify it as a resource, and activation protocols that relate it to Bell correlations. However, all these results have a limitation in common: they apply to scenarios with only one quantum party.
  Here we articulate the concept of postquantum steering for scenarios with multiple quantum parties, bringing in the missing piece to the puzzle. We provide an algorithm to certify postquantumness, which in some cases also certifies quantumness. We also define a hierarchy of semidefinite programs that bounds the set of quantum assemblages from the outside. Moreover, we show that the study of postquantum steering is fundamentally relevant since it is not just a mere mathematical curiosity allowed by the no-signalling principle, but it may arise within compositional theories beyond quantum theory. Our work further discovers a peculiarity of steering: its theory-independent description fundamentally prevents a direct connection with Bell nonlocality -- e.g., nonclassical Bell correlations do not imply nonclassical steering.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the study of postquantum steering from single-party to multi-party scenarios, developing certification algorithms, semidefinite programming hierarchies, and showing that postquantum steering is not just mathematical curiosity but may arise in compositional theories beyond quantum mechanics.
AI.motivation: Previous research on postquantum steering has been limited to single-party scenarios, leaving multi-party cases unexplored. The authors aim to address this gap by extending the concept to multiple quantum parties, providing tools for certification and analysis, and demonstrating its fundamental relevance beyond mere mathematical curiosity.
AI.method: The authors develop an algorithm to certify postquantumness in multi-party steering scenarios, define a hierarchy of semidefinite programs to bound quantum assemblages from the outside, and analyze the relationship between steering and Bell nonlocality in theory-independent frameworks.
AI.result: The work successfully extends postquantum steering to multi-party scenarios, provides practical certification tools, establishes that postquantum steering may arise in compositional theories beyond quantum mechanics, and reveals that steering's theory-independent description prevents direct connection with Bell nonlocality.
AI.conclusion: This research completes the puzzle of postquantum steering by addressing the missing multi-party case, showing that postquantum steering is fundamentally relevant and not just mathematical curiosity, while revealing important limitations in connecting steering with Bell nonlocality due to theory-independent descriptions.

title: Quantum coherent transceivers toward Holevo-limited communications
summary: The Holevo limit bounds the channel capacity of a communication channel in which information is encoded in quantum states in a Hilbert space at the transmitter and decoded using quantum measurements at the receiver. Saturating the Holevo limit requires quantum-limited transceivers that either generate quantum states of light or employ quantum-limited measurements. Here, we demonstrate an integrated photonic-electronic quantum-limited coherent receiver (QRX) achieving 14.0 dB shot noise clearance (SNC), 520 $μ$W knee power, 2.57 GHz 3-dB bandwidth, 3.50 GHz shot-noise-limited bandwidth, and 90.2 dB common-mode rejection ratio ($\mathrm{CMRR}$). We scale this design to a 32-channel QRX array with median 26.6 dB $\mathrm{SNC}$, and automatic $\mathrm{CMRR}$ correction yielding a median 76.8 dB $\mathrm{CMRR}$ at minimum. Using the integrated QRX and fiber-optic transmitter, we measure $0.15\pm0.01$ dB of squeezing below the shot noise limit, limited by off-chip losses. We propose a squeezed light communication scheme that can surpass the Shannon limit, with a path toward the Holevo limit.

AI.tldr: Demonstration of integrated photonic-electronic quantum-limited coherent receiver achieving high performance metrics and scaling to 32-channel array, enabling squeezed light communication that can surpass Shannon limit toward Holevo limit.
AI.motivation: The Holevo limit represents the ultimate capacity bound for quantum communication channels, but saturating it requires quantum-limited transceivers. Current systems lack integrated, scalable quantum-limited receivers capable of practical implementation.
AI.method: Developed an integrated photonic-electronic quantum-limited coherent receiver (QRX) with high shot noise clearance, bandwidth, and common-mode rejection. Scaled to 32-channel QRX array with automatic CMRR correction. Used integrated QRX with fiber-optic transmitter to measure squeezing below shot noise limit.
AI.result: Achieved 14.0 dB shot noise clearance, 520 μW knee power, 2.57 GHz 3-dB bandwidth, 3.50 GHz shot-noise-limited bandwidth, and 90.2 dB CMRR. 32-channel array showed median 26.6 dB SNC and 76.8 dB CMRR. Measured 0.15±0.01 dB squeezing below shot noise limit. Demonstrated path toward surpassing Shannon limit.
AI.conclusion: The integrated quantum-limited coherent receiver enables practical squeezed light communication that can surpass the classical Shannon limit, providing a pathway toward achieving the ultimate Holevo limit for quantum communication channels.

title: Continuous-variable two-dimensional cluster states in the microwave domain
summary: We demonstrate the experimental realization of two-dimensional, continuous variable (CV) cluster states between 191 microwave frequency modes. This result is obtained by exposing vacuum fluctuations to the input of a Josephson Parametric Amplifier, parametrically pumped by a sum of coherent tones around twice its resonant frequency. By carefully tuning pump frequencies, amplitudes, and phases we engineer the interference between mixing products and realize honeycomb and square lattice CV cluster states with three and four pump tones respectively. We prove the presence of the cluster states with a suitable nullifier test, reaching up to $-1.2$ dB of squeezing of the cluster state's nullifiers. We study hidden entanglement (HE) and show no hidden entanglement up to $\sim -1$ dB of squeezing and negligible HE at optimal squeezing.

AI.tldr: Experimental realization of 2D continuous variable cluster states with 191 microwave modes using Josephson Parametric Amplifier and parametric pumping, achieving up to -1.2 dB squeezing with minimal hidden entanglement.
AI.motivation: To experimentally create large-scale continuous variable cluster states in the microwave domain, which are essential resources for quantum information processing, quantum computing, and quantum networking applications.
AI.method: Used a Josephson Parametric Amplifier pumped by coherent tones around twice its resonant frequency. Engineered interference between mixing products by carefully tuning pump frequencies, amplitudes, and phases to create honeycomb and square lattice CV cluster states with three and four pump tones respectively.
AI.result: Successfully realized 2D CV cluster states between 191 microwave frequency modes. Demonstrated up to -1.2 dB of squeezing of the cluster state's nullifiers. Showed no hidden entanglement up to ~-1 dB of squeezing and negligible hidden entanglement at optimal squeezing.
AI.conclusion: The experiment demonstrates a scalable approach to generating large-scale continuous variable cluster states in the microwave domain, with well-characterized entanglement properties suitable for quantum information applications.

title: Overlapped groupings for quantum energy estimation: Maximal variance reduction and deterministic algorithms for reducing variance
summary: Grouping-based measurement strategies are widely used to reduce measurement complexity in near-term quantum algorithms. While these schemes have typically produced disjoint groups, recently this has been relaxed in what is known as overlapped grouping or coefficient splitting where operators may appear in more than one compatible group. In recent work, it has been numerically shown that this strategy can reduce the variance of energy estimates on small benchmark problems, motivating both the application and further analysis of the method. Here we prove that overlapped grouping for energy estimation can lead to a maximal variance reduction that is linear in the number of Hamiltonian terms. We introduce a new algorithm which we call repacking to transform existing groups into overlapped groups, and we show this repacking procedure iteratively reduces variance under mild assumptions. We also perform numerical simulations with Hamiltonians up to $44$ qubits and $575 \cdot 10^{3}$ terms, assessing overlapped grouping at scale on problems of practical importance. Our numerics show that the variance reduction relative to state-of-the-art (disjoint) grouping increases linearly with the problem size, suggesting that overlapped grouping methods can be a powerful strategy for quantum energy estimation at the scale of Megaquop computers and beyond.

AI.tldr: Overlapped grouping reduces variance in quantum energy estimation by allowing operators to appear in multiple compatible groups, with maximal variance reduction scaling linearly with Hamiltonian terms.
AI.motivation: Traditional grouping-based measurement strategies use disjoint groups, but overlapped grouping (coefficient splitting) has shown numerical promise for reducing variance in energy estimates on small problems, motivating both application and theoretical analysis of the method.
AI.method: The paper proves theoretical bounds on variance reduction from overlapped grouping, introduces a "repacking" algorithm to transform existing groups into overlapped groups, and performs numerical simulations on Hamiltonians up to 44 qubits with 575,000 terms to assess performance at scale.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows maximal variance reduction from overlapped grouping scales linearly with the number of Hamiltonian terms. Numerical simulations demonstrate that variance reduction relative to state-of-the-art disjoint grouping increases linearly with problem size, suggesting significant benefits for large-scale quantum energy estimation.
AI.conclusion: Overlapped grouping methods represent a powerful strategy for quantum energy estimation at scale, particularly relevant for Megaquop computers and beyond, with both theoretical guarantees and empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness.

title: Robust and High-Fidelity Controlled Two-Qubit Gates via Asymmetric Parallel Resonant Excitation
summary: Implementing high-fidelity controlled two-qubit gates in dipole-dipole interacting systems, such as rare-earth-ion crystals, in hindered by spectral inhomogeneity and weak coupling. Existing method often rely on detuned pulses, making them susceptible to frequency errors and AC Stark shifts. We propose a robust resonant scheme for arbitrary controlled two-qubit gates that utilizes asymmetric excitation and pulse engineering to achieve decoupled, parallel qubit control. Simulations on rare-earth-ion ensemble qubits demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding 99% within a 170 kHz detuning range with off-resonant excitation below 0.2%. This approach offers a robust, scalable route for quantum computing in spectrally crowded systems.

AI.tldr: Robust resonant scheme for controlled two-qubit gates in dipole-dipole interacting systems using asymmetric excitation and pulse engineering to overcome spectral inhomogeneity and weak coupling issues.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity controlled two-qubit gates in dipole-dipole interacting systems like rare-earth-ion crystals are hindered by spectral inhomogeneity and weak coupling. Existing detuned pulse methods are susceptible to frequency errors and AC Stark shifts.
AI.method: Proposes a robust resonant scheme utilizing asymmetric excitation and pulse engineering to achieve decoupled, parallel qubit control for arbitrary controlled two-qubit gates.
AI.result: Simulations on rare-earth-ion ensemble qubits demonstrate gate fidelities exceeding 99% within a 170 kHz detuning range with off-resonant excitation below 0.2%.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a robust, scalable route for quantum computing in spectrally crowded systems by overcoming limitations of existing methods.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Geometrically Local QAC0 circuits
summary:
The computational complexity of $\mathsf{QAC}^0$, which are constant-depth, polynomial-size quantum circuit families consisting of arbitrary single-qubit unitaries and $n$-qubit generalized Toffoli gates, has gained tremendous focus recently.
  In this work, we initiate the study of the computational complexity of geometrically local $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits, where all the generalized Toffoli gates act on nearest neighbor qubits. We show that any $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit can be exactly simulated by a two-dimensional geometrically local $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit, i.e., a $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^{0}$ circuit, with a quadratic size blow-up. This implies that $\mathsf{QAC}^0 = \mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^{0}$. We further show that if there existed a $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuit that computes Parity with a bounded constant error, then for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there would exist a $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^{0}$ circuit that exactly computes Parity, with a very "thin" width $n^\varepsilon$.
  We further study the computational power of $\mathsf{1D\text{-}QAC}^{0} $ circuits, i.e., one-dimensional $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits, which are the "thinnest" $\mathsf{2D\text{-}QAC}^{0}$ circuits. We prove a nearly logarithmic depth lower bound on $\mathsf{1D\text{-}QAC}^{0} $ circuits to compute the Parity function, even if allowing an unlimited number of ancilla. Furthermore, if the inputs are encoded in contiguous qubits, we prove that it requires a nearly linear depth $\mathsf{1D\text{-}QAC}^{0} $ circuit to compute the Parity function. This lower bound is almost tight. The results are proved via the combination of the restriction argument and the light-cone argument. These results may provide a new angle for studying the computational power of $\mathsf{QAC}^0$ circuits and for resolving the long-standing open problem of whether Parity is in $\mathsf{QAC}^0$.

AI.tldr: Geometrically local QAC⁰ circuits are studied, showing QAC⁰ = 2D-QAC⁰ with quadratic size blow-up, and proving strong depth lower bounds for 1D-QAC⁰ circuits computing Parity.
AI.motivation: To understand the computational complexity of geometrically local QAC⁰ circuits (constant-depth quantum circuits with arbitrary single-qubit unitaries and generalized Toffoli gates) and their relationship to the long-standing open problem of whether Parity is in QAC⁰.
AI.method: 1. Show any QAC⁰ circuit can be exactly simulated by a 2D-QAC⁰ circuit with quadratic size blow-up using geometric locality constraints. 2. Use restriction argument and light-cone argument to prove depth lower bounds for 1D-QAC⁰ circuits computing Parity.
AI.result: 1. QAC⁰ = 2D-QAC⁰ (equality of complexity classes). 2. If Parity ∈ QAC⁰ with bounded error, then for any ε>0, there exists 2D-QAC⁰ circuit computing Parity exactly with width n^ε. 3. Nearly logarithmic depth lower bound for 1D-QAC⁰ computing Parity (even with unlimited ancilla). 4. Nearly linear depth lower bound for 1D-QAC⁰ computing Parity when inputs are in contiguous qubits (almost tight).
AI.conclusion: Geometric locality constraints don't change the computational power of QAC⁰ circuits (QAC⁰ = 2D-QAC⁰), but 1D-QAC⁰ circuits have significant limitations for computing Parity. These results provide new approaches for studying QAC⁰ and the Parity problem.

title: Quantum Gibbs sampling through the detectability lemma
summary: Gibbs state preparation is an important subroutine in quantum computing. In this work we use the detectability lemma to improve Gibbs state preparation. Specifically, we design new Gibbs state preparation methods that do not rely on simulating Lindbladian evolution, thus avoiding the overhead from it. For local Lindbladians consisting of $M$ terms, this approach reduces the cost by a factor of $O(M)$. We also combine the detectability lemma operator and quantum singular value transformation to implement ground state projection operators of frustration-free Hamiltonians, resulting in a quadratic speedup in the spectral gap dependence. Applying this method to Lindbladians for the Gibbs state of local commuting Hamiltonians, we achieve quadratically better dependence on the Lindbladian spectral gap.

AI.tldr: Improved Gibbs state preparation using detectability lemma avoids Lindbladian simulation overhead, achieving O(M) cost reduction and quadratic speedup in spectral gap dependence.
AI.motivation: Gibbs state preparation is a crucial subroutine in quantum computing, but existing methods relying on Lindbladian evolution simulation incur significant overhead that needs to be reduced.
AI.method: Uses detectability lemma to design Gibbs state preparation methods that avoid simulating Lindbladian evolution. Combines detectability lemma operator with quantum singular value transformation to implement ground state projection operators of frustration-free Hamiltonians.
AI.result: For local Lindbladians with M terms, reduces cost by factor O(M). Achieves quadratic speedup in spectral gap dependence for Gibbs states of local commuting Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: The detectability lemma provides significant improvements for Gibbs state preparation, eliminating Lindbladian simulation overhead and achieving better scaling with spectral gaps.

title: Fock State Generation and SWAP using a Rabi-Driven Qubit
summary: The deterministic generation and SWAP of Fock states in isolated high-Q modes form a core foundation for architectures in bosonic quantum computing. Conventionally, these operations necessitate strong coupling to a qubit, which inherently compromises the required cavity isolation. To address this trade-off, we introduce a tunable mechanism wherein a weakly coupled qubit, which preserves mode isolation, is driven to induce a strong interaction on demand. By leveraging a Rabi-driven, qubit-mediated sideband interaction, we realize on-demand Jaynes-Cummings coupling between a transmon and a long-lived cavity mode. Using a superconducting flute cavity with two high-Q modes, we deterministically demonstrate Fock state preparation up to n=5 at operation times of less than 2 microseconds per photon. We also demonstrate and characterize single-photon SWAP in approximately 2 microseconds. Finally, we adapt our SWAP method to generate a dual-rail Bell state. While current performance is constrained by baseline coherence rather than fundamental methodological limits, the protocol scales inherently to accommodate higher photon numbers and faster operational regimes. By enabling complex operations on modes that remain strictly weakly coupled to qubits, this approach establishes a robust pathway for advancing scalable bosonic quantum computing.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates deterministic Fock state generation and photon SWAP in high-Q cavities using a weakly coupled qubit with on-demand strong interaction, enabling scalable bosonic quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Traditional Fock state generation requires strong qubit-cavity coupling that compromises cavity isolation. Need a method that preserves high-Q mode isolation while enabling strong interactions on demand.
AI.method: Uses a weakly coupled transmon qubit driven to induce strong interaction via Rabi-driven, qubit-mediated sideband interaction. Implements on-demand Jaynes-Cummings coupling between transmon and long-lived cavity mode in superconducting flute cavity with two high-Q modes.
AI.result: Deterministic Fock state preparation up to n=5 with operation times <2 μs per photon. Single-photon SWAP in ~2 μs. Generation of dual-rail Bell state. Performance limited by baseline coherence, not fundamental methodological limits.
AI.conclusion: Protocol enables complex operations on weakly coupled modes, establishing scalable pathway for bosonic quantum computing. Scales inherently to higher photon numbers and faster operations.

title: Quantifying and detecting quantum-state texture
summary: Quantum-state texture is a recently proposed quantum resource that characterizes the inhomogeneity of a quantum state's matrix element distribution in the computational basis, enriching our understanding of quantum state structure. To expand its quantification toolkit and establish detection methods, in this article, we investigate the resource theory of texture from both quantitative and detection perspectives. First, we construct a texture measure $\mathcal{T}^{\text{GR}}_{α,z}(ρ)$ based on the $α$-$z$ Rényi relative entropy and present some of its inherent properties. Second, we analyze the mathematical relationships between several existing texture measures, revealing connections among different quantifiers. Finally, drawing on the witness concept from other resource theories, we systematically introduce texture witnesses into the texture theory and provide examples of texture witnesses with special properties.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a resource theory for quantum-state texture, constructing new texture measures based on Rényi relative entropy, analyzing relationships between existing measures, and introducing texture witnesses for detection.
AI.motivation: To expand the quantification toolkit for quantum-state texture (a resource characterizing inhomogeneity of quantum state matrix element distribution) and establish detection methods, enriching understanding of quantum state structure.
AI.method: 1) Construct texture measure $\mathcal{T}^{\text{GR}}_{α,z}(ρ)$ based on α-z Rényi relative entropy and analyze its properties; 2) Analyze mathematical relationships between existing texture measures; 3) Systematically introduce texture witnesses into texture theory with examples of witnesses having special properties.
AI.result: Developed a new texture measure based on Rényi relative entropy, revealed connections between different texture quantifiers, and established a framework for texture witnesses for detection purposes.
AI.conclusion: The paper advances the resource theory of quantum-state texture by providing new quantification tools, clarifying relationships between measures, and introducing detection methods via texture witnesses, thereby enhancing the theoretical framework for studying this quantum resource.

title: Physics-Informed Discrete-Event Simulation of Polarization-Encoded Quantum Networks
comment: 10 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to IEEE Quantum Week (QCE) 2026. Code available upon request
summary: We extend the SeQUeNCe discrete-event simulator with physics-based models for polarization-encoded photonic quantum networks. Our framework integrates Jones-calculus optical components, including an SPDC Bell-state source, wave plates, and polarizing beam splitters, together with a multi-section fiber model capturing polarization mode dispersion, chromatic dispersion, and Raman noise from coexisting classical traffic. We validate the simulator by reproducing experimentally reported spectra, polarization correlations, quantum state tomography, and dispersion- and Raman-induced noise. The resulting platform enables hardware-parameterized prediction of entanglement distribution performance under realistic deployment conditions.

AI.tldr: Extension of SeQUeNCe simulator with physics-based models for polarization-encoded photonic quantum networks, incorporating Jones-calculus optical components and fiber effects for realistic performance prediction.
AI.motivation: To enable hardware-parameterized prediction of entanglement distribution performance in polarization-encoded photonic quantum networks under realistic deployment conditions by incorporating physics-based models into existing simulation frameworks.
AI.method: Extended the SeQUeNCe discrete-event simulator with Jones-calculus optical components (SPDC Bell-state source, wave plates, polarizing beam splitters) and a multi-section fiber model capturing polarization mode dispersion, chromatic dispersion, and Raman noise from coexisting classical traffic.
AI.result: Validated the simulator by reproducing experimentally reported spectra, polarization correlations, quantum state tomography, and dispersion- and Raman-induced noise, creating a platform for hardware-parameterized performance prediction.
AI.conclusion: The developed framework enables realistic simulation and performance prediction of polarization-encoded photonic quantum networks under practical deployment conditions, bridging the gap between theoretical models and experimental implementations.

title: Rotation of the Transition Dipole in Single hBN Quantum Emitters via Vibronic Coupling
summary: The design of polarization-encoded quantum interfaces relies on the assumption that solid-state emitters possess static transition dipoles defined by the host lattice symmetry. Here, we demonstrate the vibronic breakdown of this static dipole approximation in hexagonal boron nitride quantum emitters. Through high-resolution energy-resolved spectroscopy, we reveal a continuous, spectral rotation of the emission dipole orientation reaching up to 40$^{\circ}$, driven by coupling to the phonon bath. This spectral gradient is significantly suppressed at cryogenic temperatures (6 K), identifying thermally activated lattice vibrations as the primary driver of the dipole reorientation. First-principles calculations on two representative defect types indicate the microscopic origin of this phenomenon as a coordinate-dependent transition dipole, where phonon-induced atomic displacements fundamentally perturb the electronic wavefunctions. By comparing the distinct defect environments, we demonstrate that the magnitude of the polarization rotation scales with the strength of the vibronic coupling. Our results not only identify a fundamental limit for polarization fidelity in solid-state quantum networks but also suggest a new class of strain-tunable quantum photonic devices based on vibronic dipole reorientation.

AI.tldr: Quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride show spectral rotation of emission dipole orientation up to 40°, driven by phonon coupling, challenging the static dipole approximation for polarization-encoded quantum interfaces.
AI.motivation: The design of polarization-encoded quantum interfaces assumes static transition dipoles defined by host lattice symmetry, but this static dipole approximation may break down in solid-state emitters.
AI.method: Used high-resolution energy-resolved spectroscopy to measure emission dipole orientation, combined with cryogenic temperature measurements (6 K) and first-principles calculations on two representative defect types in hexagonal boron nitride.
AI.result: Revealed continuous spectral rotation of emission dipole orientation reaching up to 40°, driven by coupling to phonon bath; rotation significantly suppressed at cryogenic temperatures; magnitude scales with vibronic coupling strength.
AI.conclusion: Identifies fundamental limit for polarization fidelity in solid-state quantum networks and suggests new class of strain-tunable quantum photonic devices based on vibronic dipole reorientation.

title: Interaction-Mediated Non-Reciprocal Dynamics in Open Quantum Systems: From an Exactly Solvable Model to Generic Behavior
summary: Reservoir engineering has emerged as a powerful paradigm to realize non-reciprocal dynamics in open quantum many-body systems. Here, we show that density-density interactions can transfer bath-induced non-reciprocity between different degrees of freedom. Specifically, we investigate a one-dimensional lattice of spin-$\frac{1}{2}$ fermions with all-to-all Hatsugai-Kohmoto interactions in the presence of an engineered reservoir. We establish the exact solvability of the Lindbladian dynamics and show that the interplay between non-reciprocity and interactions qualitatively reshapes the dynamics of excitations. Remarkably, interactions induce directional drift even in spin sectors that are not directly coupled to the reservoir. By analyzing a driven-dissipative Fermi-Hubbard chain, we show that the same mechanism persists for local interactions. The Hatsugai-Kohmoto model thus emerges as a minimal, exactly solvable platform for interaction-mediated non-reciprocal many-body dynamics.

AI.tldr: Interactions transfer bath-induced non-reciprocity between degrees of freedom in open quantum systems, enabling directional drift in spin sectors not directly coupled to reservoirs.
AI.motivation: To understand how density-density interactions can transfer bath-induced non-reciprocity between different degrees of freedom in open quantum many-body systems, and to establish exactly solvable models for studying interaction-mediated non-reciprocal dynamics.
AI.method: Study a 1D lattice of spin-1/2 fermions with all-to-all Hatsugai-Kohmoto interactions in an engineered reservoir, establishing exact solvability of Lindbladian dynamics. Also analyze a driven-dissipative Fermi-Hubbard chain to show mechanism persists for local interactions.
AI.result: Interactions qualitatively reshape excitation dynamics by inducing directional drift in spin sectors not directly coupled to the reservoir. The Hatsugai-Kohmoto model provides an exactly solvable platform for interaction-mediated non-reciprocal many-body dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Density-density interactions can transfer bath-induced non-reciprocity between different degrees of freedom, enabling interaction-mediated non-reciprocal dynamics in open quantum many-body systems, with the Hatsugai-Kohmoto model serving as a minimal exactly solvable platform.
